paragraphs.text: Here's a small app built with lit HTML. A number, and a button that adds one to it.

Open the browser's developer tools, and you'll find a few things in the DOM that you didn't write. An empty comment. And a comment with a strange name: lit, and a long random number, between dollar signs.
Where do they come from? Let's follow one template all the way through lit HTML, from the code you write, to the moment the number on the screen changes.
Here's the code. The counter function takes a number, and returns a template with three expressions in it: the span's class, the number itself, and a click handler.
We render it once with zero. And each click renders it again, with the next number.
Inside lit HTML, rendering has three phases: prepare, create, and update. Much of what makes lit HTML fast is how often it gets to skip the first two.

Let's start with the template itself. The word html, right before the backtick, makes this a tagged template literal. When it runs, JavaScript splits it into two lists: the fixed strings of HTML, and the values of the expressions in between. Then it calls the html function, with both.

And html does almost nothing with them. It returns a plain object, holding the strings, the values, and a number that says this is HTML. That object is called a template result. Nothing has been parsed, and the DOM hasn't been touched.
Now, call counter again, with one. The values are new. But the strings array isn't. It's the very same object as before.

JavaScript makes one strings array for each template literal in your code, and passes that same array every time the literal runs. So the array itself makes a perfect cache key. Same strings array, same template.

Now we render. First, render checks the container for a part it left there on an earlier render. This is the first render, so there isn't one. So it makes one: a child part, and it marks where that part begins with an empty comment. That's the first mystery comment.
A child part manages a spot in the DOM that can hold content: text, nodes, a list, or a whole template. It's stored on the container, for next time, and then it's given our template result.

The first thing the part does is look up the template. lit HTML keeps a cache of prepared templates, keyed by the strings array. This one has never been rendered, so it isn't there. In fact, until this moment, lit HTML hasn't looked at this template's HTML at all. Now it has to prepare it.

Preparing turns the strings into DOM. lit HTML doesn't include an HTML parser. It uses the browser's, which is fast, and handles every corner of HTML. But a parser needs complete HTML, and our strings have holes in them. So first, lit HTML fills each hole with a marker, one it can find again after parsing.

Which marker to use depends on where the hole is. So lit HTML scans the strings, but it doesn't build anything. It tracks just enough to know whether it's in text, inside a tag, or inside an attribute's value. A handful of regular expressions is all that takes.

The first hole is in the value of the class attribute. lit HTML puts the marker in the value, and adds dollar, lit, dollar, to the attribute's name. That makes the binding easy to find later, and the browser never sees a real class attribute full of marker text.

The second hole is in text, inside the span. Here, the marker goes between angle brackets, after a question mark. That's the syntax for a processing instruction, which HTML doesn't support, so the parser turns it into a comment. It's a few bytes shorter than writing out a comment.
The third hole is the event binding. That's another attribute value, so it's handled just like the first.
The marker itself is the word lit, and a random number, between dollar signs. The number is picked once, when the page loads, so it's very unlikely to appear in your templates by accident.
With the markers in, the strings join into one complete piece of HTML. lit HTML creates a template element, and sets its inner HTML to that string. The browser parses it into DOM.
The contents of a template element are inert. Scripts don't run, images don't load, and custom elements don't upgrade. It's DOM that's only there to be copied.
Next, lit HTML walks the new DOM once, counting nodes as it goes. It only visits elements and comments, so text nodes, like all of this whitespace, aren't counted.
Node zero is the span, and it has a bound attribute. So lit HTML records a template part: an attribute part named class, at node zero. Then it removes the attribute.
Node one is the marker comment. That's a child part, at node one. The comment stays. It'll be needed later.

Node two is the button. Its bound attribute starts with an at sign, so it's an event part, for click. A dot would make it a property part, and a question mark, a boolean attribute part. Recorded, and removed.
Three holes, three template parts, so the walk can stop.

The template element and its list of parts together make a Template, and it goes into the cache, under the strings array. That's the prepare phase. It runs once for each template literal in your code, no matter how many times, or in how many places, you render it.
Back in the root part. Is it already showing an instance of this template? No, it's empty. So it's time for phase two: create.
lit HTML makes a template instance, and clones the template's content, with import node. That's fast. The browser copies the nodes without parsing anything.

Then it walks the copy, counting nodes the same way, and stops at each index in the parts list. There, it creates a part: a small object that holds a direct reference to that node. An attribute part for the span. A child part that starts at the comment. And an event part for the button.
From now on, lit HTML never has to search for these places again.
Now, phase three: update. The instance gives each of its parts the matching value.
The attribute part gets an empty string. Its last value was nothing, so this is a change, and it sets the class attribute.
The child part gets zero. It creates a text node, and inserts it right after its comment.
The event part gets the click handler. It adds an event listener, but the listener it adds is itself. When a click comes in, the part calls whichever function it was given most recently.
All of this happens while the copy is still detached from the page. Then the root part inserts it, all at once, and remembers which instance it's showing.
And there's the second mystery comment. It's the marker from the template, copied into the page, where it marks the start of the child part.
Now, click the button. counter runs with one, and makes a new template result: the same strings array, with new values.
render finds the part it left on the body. The template is already in the cache, and the part is already showing an instance of it. So prepare and create are both skipped. Straight to update.

The class changed, from empty to odd. That's one call to set attribute. The number changed too, but lit HTML doesn't make a new text node. It changes the text of the one it made last time. And the click handler is a new function, so the part just keeps it. The listener on the button stays the same.
That's two small writes to the DOM. Nothing else in the template is touched, or even looked at. And when a string or a number hasn't changed, its part skips the DOM entirely.
A child part can hold a whole template, too. It handles one exactly the way the root part did: it looks up the template, creates an instance if it needs one, and updates it.

If the part gets a different template than last time, it clears out what's there, and creates a new instance. Switching back skips prepare, since that template is in the cache, but it does create the instance again. If you switch back and forth a lot, the cache directive keeps both instances around.
Give a child part an array, and it makes a child part for each item, each one marked by a pair of empty comments. That's where the rest of the empty comments come from.
Here, three list items come from one template literal. It's prepared once, and each item gets its own instance.
On the next render, items are matched up by position, and each instance is updated in place. To match items by a key instead, so their DOM moves when the list is reordered, use the repeat directive.
So that's the whole trip. Let's stack up the caching.

JavaScript gives each template literal one strings array. lit HTML uses that array as a key, so each template is scanned and parsed only once. Each child part remembers the instance it's showing, so DOM is only cloned when the template in that spot changes. And each part remembers its last value, so an unchanged string or number never touches the DOM.

And those comments? The empty ones are markers that lit HTML creates as it renders: for the root part, and for list items. The ones with lit and a number are the template's markers, copied into the page. Each one marks where a child part starts.
For more detail, read Life of a lit HTML render, in the lit repository, and the source, lit HTML dot T S. It's well commented, and it's all in one file.
